title: What If an Immortal Snail Was Chasing You? 🐌
description:
Gus gets a billion dollars, and a snail that can't die will crawl after him forever: one touch and it's game over. His wife laughs, his neighbor steps over it, and then Gus tries to sleep.

The numbers:
• The fastest snail ever timed (Archie, World Snail Racing Championships, Congham, England, 1995) covered a 13-inch (33 cm) course in 2 minutes: 2.75 mm a second, 0.006 mph.
• A walker at 3 mph is about 490 times faster. One 70 cm step takes the snail a little over 4 minutes.
• But the snail never stops. At that pace, around the clock: 87 yards (79 m) in an 8-hour night, 260 yards (238 m) a day, 54 miles (87 km) a year.
• A 3-minute walk at 3 mph covers the snail's whole day.
• New York to London is about 3,440 miles (5,540 km): 64 years of crawling.
• A tap dripping once a second (0.25 mL a drip) loses 21.6 litres a day and fills a 40-gallon bathtub in a week.
(Assumptions, all generous to the snail: it keeps the record pace 24 hours a day in a straight line and crosses the ocean on the shortest path. A real garden snail does about 1 mm a second and rests most of the day. Bigger tubs take up to 12 days.)
• Snails really do hitch rides: inspectors find them on shipping containers and in air passengers' luggage.

Sources:
• Guinness World Records, "Fastest snail racing" (33 cm in 2 min 00 s, 1995)
• Murtagh et al., Sports Medicine (2021): usual walking pace of adults, 1.31 m/s
• USGS Water Science School, drip calculator (0.25 mL a drip, 15,140 drips to the gallon)
• Great-circle distance JFK to LHR, haversine formula on the airports' coordinates
• USDA APHIS and US Customs and Border Protection on hitchhiking snails in cargo and luggage

Every number is computed in code and checked. Animation, narration and music are made with software and AI tools.
